Project:
A Python command-line checkers move generator and minimax game solver that reads an 8x8 board from a file, runs adversarial search, and writes successive board states to an output file.

Overview:
Implements a simplified American checkers engine with board state modeling, move generation, mandatory jump handling, piece promotion, and alpha-beta minimax search. The engine alternates turns between red and black pieces until one side has no legal pieces remaining.
Tech Stack:

Python 3
Standard library only: argparse, copy, sys, time
Architecture:

Board class stores an 8x8 matrix of chars and provides display semantics.
State encapsulates current board, turn, and search depth.
Move generation includes normal diagonal moves, forced captures, multi-jump chaining, and king movement rules.
alpha_beta_search coordinates adversarial search using max_value/min_value with alpha-beta pruning.
Static evaluation combines piece values, center control, mobility, safety, positional advantage, distance penalties, and chain-jump potential.
Challenges:

Handling exponential branching from jumps and move generation in checkers.
Representing recursive multi-jump capture sequences correctly.
Designing a heuristic evaluation function that balances material, positional control, promotion threats, and capture potential.
Performance constraints from repeated copy.deepcopy of board matrices and Python recursion at search depth.
Outcomes:

Works as a self-contained solver for input-driven checkers board states.
Uses depth-limited alpha-beta pruning at fixed depth_limit = 7.
Produces deterministic move sequences in an output file without networking or external services.
Project: Galaxy-Identifier

Overview: Desktop application that performs object detection and segmentation on astronomical images to classify galaxy morphologies using a YOLO-based model trained on Galaxy Zoo dataset with custom data augmentation techniques including noise injection, padding, and image stitching to prevent overfitting and simulate real-world variations.
Tech Stack: Python 3.11, Ultralytics YOLO (v8/v11), PyTorch 2.7.1 with TorchVision 0.22.1, Kivy 2.3.1 for GUI, OpenCV 4.11.0 for image processing, galaxy-datasets library for data loading, scikit-learn for train-test split, PIL for image handling.

Architecture: Modular pipeline with data preprocessing script converting Galaxy Zoo CSV labels to YOLO annotation format, augmentation module generating synthetic variations, YOLO training script using SGD optimizer with batch size 32 and image size 640x640, inference class wrapping YOLO model for detection, Kivy-based desktop app with tkinter file dialog for image input and real-time result display via NumPy array to PIL conversion. Containerized with Docker using Python 3.11-slim base image.
Challenges: Converting multi-label Galaxy Zoo classifications to single-class YOLO format, handling class imbalance in astronomical datasets, implementing custom augmentations without disrupting morphological features, integrating YOLO inference with Kivy UI event loop, managing memory for large image batches during training.

Outcomes: Achieved trained YOLO model for 8 galaxy morphology classes (smooth_round, unbarred_spiral, etc.), interactive application enabling user image upload and instant detection visualization, data augmentation increased training set diversity by synthetic generation techniques.
Based on the notebook, here's a focused technical summary optimized for semantic search and RAG retrieval:
Project: Image Colorization - CIFAR-10 Horse Classification

Overview:
Automated colorization of grayscale images using deep neural networks. Converts single-channel grayscale input to multi-channel color predictions via pixel-wise discrete color classification. Trained on 50,000 CIFAR-10 horse images (category 7), outputting per-pixel color category predictions that map to RGB values. Formulates colorization as supervised multi-class classification rather than regression.
Tech Stack:

PyTorch (nn.Sequential, nn.Conv2d, nn.ConvTranspose2d, nn.BatchNorm2d, nn.ReLU)
CIFAR-10 dataset (32×32 RGB images, 50K train / 10K test)
k-means color clustering (24 discrete color categories pre-computed)
NumPy for tensor manipulation
PIL for image I/O
Adam optimizer (lr=0.001)
CrossEntropyLoss (multi-class pixel-wise classification)
Architecture:
Two comparable encoder-decoder designs:

PoolUpsampleNet: Conv2d (1→32→64 filters) + MaxPool2d stride-2 downsampling in encoder; Conv2d upsampling with nn.Upsample scale_factor=2 in decoder.
ConvTransposeNet: Conv2d (1→32→64) with stride=2 downsampling in encoder; ConvTranspose2d with stride=2, output_padding=1 for learnable upsampling in decoder.
Both: 32×32 input → bottleneck (64 filters at 8×8) → 32×32 output. BatchNorm after each conv layer. 5-block total depth. Input: 1-channel grayscale or 3-channel downsampled RGB. Output: 24-channel color category logits.
Challenges:

Discrete color representation requires post-hoc mapping of network output (argmax classification indices) to RGB values via k-means codebook lookup; loses color continuity across pixels
32×32 image resolution constrains spatial detail; stride-2 operations create 2×2 bottleneck
Pixel-wise classification with 24 categories at 1024 pixels per image = 24,576-way classification problem per batch; requires loss tensor reshaping to [batch×1024, 24] for CrossEntropyLoss compatibility
Small receptive field limits context for color consistency; stride-2 convolutions and upsampling must recover fine spatial detail
Outcomes:

Training loop: 25 epochs, batch_size=100, convergence tracking via train/validation loss and per-pixel accuracy
Model serialization via torch.save checkpoint support
Visualization pipeline generates per-epoch output PNG comparisons (grayscale input vs. ground-truth vs. predicted colorization)
Activation map extraction for debugging network layer responses

Project:
Labrador is an image labeling and dataset packaging platform with a React Native/Expo mobile frontend and an Express/Prisma backend for uploading, annotating, verifying, and exporting image data.
Overview:

Users upload images from a mobile app, create bounding-box annotations, and submit images for verification.
Role-based access controls separate normal users from cashier/manager/admin users for verification and dataset management.
The backend stores images, annotations, verifications, organizations, and user validity metadata.
The current ML verification path is stubbed as a placeholder and can be replaced with a real model.
Tech Stack:

Backend: Node.js, Express 5, Prisma ORM, JWT auth, multer file upload, bcrypt, cors, dotenv.
Database: Prisma schema targets PostgreSQL via DATABASE_URL but package includes sqlite3, suggesting local dev with SQLite and deployment config with Postgres.
Frontend/mobile: Expo, React Native, React Navigation, Axios.
Storage: local filesystem uploads under backend/uploads/images/; comments indicate planned migration to Firebase/S3.
Authentication/authorization: JSON Web Tokens, role middleware, active user checks.
Architecture:

Mobile app calls REST API endpoints under /auth, /user, /organization, /image.
/image routes include upload, user image query, cashier-only pending/all image lists, annotation CRUD, verification, and ML verification.
Prisma models define User, Profile, Organization, Image, Annotation, ImageVerification, Dataset, PointsTransaction.
Image records cascade-delete annotations/verifications; organization relationship can set null on delete.
Express serves uploaded media statically under /uploads.
Challenges:

Managing image upload integrity with multipart file handling and validation via multer.
Enforcing role-based permissions across a mixed user/verification workflow.
Keeping annotation and verification data consistent when images are deleted.
Supporting both per-user and organization-scoped images while preserving access control.
Designing dataset export support for CV formats like COCO/YOLO/Pascal VOC without current implementation.
Outcomes:

Provides a complete labeled-image ingestion pipeline with structured metadata for computer vision training.
Implements a verification workflow that updates image approval state and calculates user validity percentage.
Enables cashier/manager roles to review pending images and validate annotations before dataset packaging.
Lays groundwork for ML-assisted verification and future scalable storage/back-end migration.

Project:
Neutral Machine Translation Model

Overview:
Character-level neural machine translation system that translates English words to Pig Latin using a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture. The model operates at individual character granularity rather than word level, requiring the attention mechanisms to align character-by-character transformations. Core task: learn linguistic transformation rules through supervised learning on parallel English-Pig Latin word pairs.
Tech Stack:

PyTorch (deep learning framework)
Python

NumPy, Matplotlib, Pandas
Architecture:
Stacked multi-layer transformer with two distinct components:

TransformerEncoder: Self-attention over input characters, scaled dot-product attention, sine/cosine positional encodings (Vaswani et al.), residual connections, feed-forward MLPs per layer
TransformerDecoder: Causal self-attention (prevents attending to future tokens), cross-attention over encoder annotations, identical positional encoding scheme, multi-layer stacking with residual pathways
Embedding layer: Character-to-dense-vector transformation
Output layer: Linear projection to vocabulary logits, softmax for token probabilities
Special tokens: SOS (start), EOS (end), EOP (end of prompt)
Challenges:

Character-level sequence generation requires precise positional attention; single misaligned character breaks output validity
Causal masking in decoder prevents attending beyond current position, limiting context for generating subsequent characters
Batch bucketing by (source_length, target_length) pairs adds preprocessing complexity; sparse buckets waste computation
Positional encoding design must scale to variable-length inputs (max_seq_len=1000)
Model must implicitly learn Pig Latin rules (vowel movements, consonant clusters) from data without explicit rules
Outcomes:

Multiple trained variants with configurable hyperparameters (hidden_size: 32/64, num_layers: 3/4, batch_size: 64/512)
Training curves tracked per-epoch on small and large datasets (pig_latin_small.txt, pig_latin_large.txt)
Validation loss monitoring with early stopping (patience configurable)
Qualitative translation outputs per epoch on test sentence ("the air conditioning is working")
Attention weight visualization per decoder layer showing alignment between input and output characters
Checkpoint saving of best models (encoder, decoder, vocabulary mappings)

# Project

Labrador is a client-heavy semantic search and RAG prototype for a React portfolio website. The frontend generates user queries and sends them to a mocked backend API (api/chat.js). In-browser embedding logic and OpenRouter API integration are being developed.

---

## Overview

User queries are embedded (planned in-browser) and used for nearest-neighbor retrieval over a precomputed vector index. The backend composes contextual prompts for an LLM to generate final answers. During development, a mock API simulates retrieval and LLM orchestration.

---

## Tech Stack

Frontend uses React (Vite) with client-side JavaScript for embedding.

The backend is a Node.js serverless API route (api/chat.js placeholder).

Embeddings are generated using a client-side model (WebAssembly/ONNX or remote embedding API).

The LLM layer uses OpenAI mini 5.4.

Infrastructure is deployed on Vercel using serverless hosting.

---

## Architecture

In-browser processing tokenizes and embeds queries before sending vectors (or raw queries) to the backend.

The backend performs vector database lookup using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, retrieves top-k chunks, filters results, and assembles a prompt context for the LLM.

The indexing pipeline includes document chunking, embedding generation, metadata storage, and periodic reindexing.

---

## Important Technical Decisions

Embedding can be performed in-browser for privacy and latency or on the server for consistency and reduced client complexity.

The system uses ANN indexing (HNSW or IVF+PQ) for scalable low-latency retrieval.

A hybrid retrieval approach combines lexical search (BM25) with dense vector search to improve precision.

Context window management and chunk sizing are optimized to prevent prompt overflow.

Each retrieval result includes provenance metadata such as source IDs and offsets for traceability.

---

## Challenges

Client-side constraints such as CPU usage, memory limits, and model size impact in-browser embedding performance.

API key security must balance between client exposure and serverless execution.

Index freshness requires strategies for incremental updates as documents change.

Long documents and near-duplicate chunks require careful chunking and overlap tuning.

LLM cost and latency require batching, caching, and strict context filtering.

Evaluation requires building relevance labels and measuring retrieval quality using metrics like recall@k and MRR.

---

## Outcomes

The system improves semantic recall compared to keyword search by capturing paraphrases and intent-based queries.

Expected improvements include higher recall@k, improved MRR, and reduced time-to-answer.

Retrieval provenance enables explainability and supports user-facing citations and auditing.
